Premature infants are infants born before 37 weeks' gestation.
Very low-birth-weight (VLBW) infants are less than 1500 g.
Extremely low-birth-weight (ELBW) infants are less than 1000 g.
The incidence of premature births is increasing. In the United States, 13% of all infants are born premature.
Two percent of premature infants are born before 32 weeks' gestation.
With the improvements in neonatal care, there has been a corresponding increase in survival of these infants.

section.type: Components of Discharge Planning for Premature Infants
section.heading: Components of Discharge Planning for Premature Infants

list.listitem: Discharge planning and follow-up are critical to ensure a successful transition home for infant and family.
Assure that the infant is safe to be discharged home and is physiologically stable.

Consider performing a car seat challenge. This involves monitoring the infant with continuous pulse oximetry in their car seat prior to discharge for any respiratory compromise, which may require a different type of car seat.

Involve the family early in the care of their infant. Parents who are actively involved with their infant's care in the NICU demonstrate greater confidence in handling the infant and are more prepared to assume full responsibility for care at home.
Arrange a follow-up appointment with the primary care physician. Provide the primary care physician with a complete summary of the infant's NICU course and follow-up needs.
Arrange follow-up specialty appointments for unresolved medical issues (ie, ophthalmology follow-up for ROP).
Arrange follow-up surveillance and support services (ie, neurodevelopmental follow-up, occupational therapy, physical therapy, etc).
Regularly monitor nutrition and growth by plotting weight, length, and head circumference using the infant's corrected age and growth charts designed for the premature infant.

The nutritional needs of the premature infant are greater than those of an infant born at term, with increased protein, calorie, and mineral requirements. Most infants require 100 to 120 kcal/kg/d to achieve the desired weight gain of 20 to 30 grams/day. Infants with increased metabolic needs like chronic lung disease may require more than 150 kcal/kg/d.

Breast milk is the preferred choice for feeding all infants. In addition to its nutrient properties, breast milk provides protection from infection, is better tolerated, and promotes maternal-infant bonding. Although several early studies suggested improved cognitive outcomes in breast-fed infants, recent evidence is less persuasive.
Supplement exclusively breast-fed infants with iron (2-4 mg/kg/d) and Vitamin D (400 IU/d).

For infants less than 1500 g, fortify breast milk to provide the increased requirements for calories, protein, and minerals. Fortified breast milk feeding is associated with short-term improvement in weight gain, as well as linear and head growth.

Infants who are not breastfed should continue with specially developed postdischarge formulas to ensure ongoing optimal growth and development. Although initial studies suggested improvements in growth with the postdischarge formulas, a Cochrane review comparing these formulas to term formulas showed no difference in growth or neurodevelopmental outcome.

For preterm or low birth weight infants unable to be breast fed, a Cochrane review concluded based on 12 randomized trials with 1879 patients that feeding with formula, compared to donor breast milk, results in better growth (linear, head, and weight gain) but also a higher risk of necrotising enterocolitis (risk difference 3%, 95% CI 1 to 5%, NNH = 33).

Cochrane reviews evaluated randomized trials of the effect of carbohydrate, fat, and protein supplementation of human breast milk in preterm and low birthweight infants. Overall, the quality and quantity of evidence was low, with limited evidence that protein supplementation results in short-term increases in growth and no evidence to support carbohydrate or fat supplementation.
Premature infants are at increased risk of neurodevelopmental abnormalities due to insults to the developing brain, including intraventricular hemorrhage and ischemia.
Refer premature infants to a developmental follow-up program.

A Cochrane review found that early intervention programs for premature infants improved cognitive outcomes during infancy and preschool age, but these improved outcomes did not extend to school age. Early intervention programs were associated with a small improvement in motor outcomes in infancy, that did not extend to preschool or school age. However, there were few studies that followed motor outcomes to preschool or school age.

During the first 2 years of life, assess neurodevelopment using standardized developmental assessment tools based on corrected age. Refer appropriately for any identified abnormality. See chapter on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities.
Immunize premature infants according to the recommended schedule for term infants using their chronological age.
Give the first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine after the infant is more than 2000 g.

Give the influenza vaccine for all infants more than 6 months old. For optimal protection, infants should receive 2 influenza vaccinations separated by 4 weeks. All family members of infants less than 6 months of age should also receive the influenza vaccine.

Give RSV immunoglobulin (Palivizumab [Synagis]) monthly during RSV season for infants born at less than 29 weeks gestation and for infants born at less than 32 weeks gestation who have chronic lung disease requiring supplemental oxygen. It decreases the rate of hospitalization attributable to RSV in premature infants by 45% to 55%. See .
Give RSV monoclonal antibody (Nirsevimab) to all infants less than 8 months of age during or before their first RSV season.

Premature infants are at risk for ROP. This is a condition that occurs in VLBW infants and ELBW infants because of disruption of the growth of the retinal vessels, leading to vascular proliferation of varying degrees. This may result in retinal detachment. Depending on the stage of ROP identified, these children may develop significant vision abnormalities including strabismus, refractive errors, and even blindness.
All infants born at less than 32 weeks' gestation are routinely screened for ROP at 4 to 6 weeks postdelivery. On the basis of the findings, follow-up with an ophthalmologist as directed.

Topical proparacaine ophthalmic drops 30 seconds prior to an ophthalmic examination for ROP decreases pain associated with the ophthalmic exam (fewer infants with an increase in the Premature Infant Pain Profile (PIPP) score greater than 4 from baseline scores; RR: 0.70; 95% CI: 0.52-0.94; RD −0.19; 95% CI: −0.34 to −0.04; NNTB 5.3), but the examination continues to be a painful procedure and additional research is needed to further reduce pain associated with the screening exam.
Five percent of infants born before 32 weeks' gestation will have hearing loss diagnosed by 5 years of age.
Early recognition of hearing impairment and appropriate intervention are critical to ensure that the child achieves optimal language development.
All premature infants should be screened for hearing loss prior to discharge from the NICU.
Ongoing screening after discharge should be arranged and any concerns about speech or hearing from caregivers must be investigated and appropriate referrals made.
